newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin, Kohl to repair Franco-German euro-motor.
newsitem.headline: Jospin, Kohl to repair Franco-German euro-motor.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin have set a date to clear the air in Franco-German relations in what could be a decisive step on the road to a single European currency.
They are to meet on August 28 in Bonn to try to overcome strains in ties between two countries which pride themselves on working together as the motor of European integration.

Ever since the French left won an upset election victory on June 1, raising doubts about Paris' willingness to make more sacrifices for the euro, political analysts and financial markets have been awaiting this moment of truth.

The "clarification" between a battered, conservative chancellor, widely seen as in the twilight of his power, and a Socialist premier, keen to mark his independence from Bonn and difference from conservative President Jacques Chirac, is seen as essential to keep EU economic and monetary union on track.
"They are doomed to succeed," said a European diplomat who follows Franco-German relations closely. "The fate of the euro rides on Kohl and Jospin finding a common way forward."

A French official said he expected a strong statement of their shared determination to launch the euro on time in January 1999, to make another push for closer European political integration and perhaps to revamp the 1963 Franco-German treaty.

The vital talks, nearly three months after Jospin's election stripped Chirac of much of his power, will take place after both Germany and France have taken steps to reduce overrunning budget deficits to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Bonn announced a package of tax hikes, spending cuts and asset sales last Friday to try to reach its own strict "3.0" interpretation of the Maastricht treaty goal of limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.

Jospin's government was meeting on Thursday to finalise tax and savings measures to be announced next Monday, when an indepedent audit is expected to show this year's French deficit is running at more than 3.5 percent of GDP.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has said Paris won't make "3.0" percent but it will make an effort to bring down this year's deficit and meet the target next year.

One of Kohl's closest party associates, Christian Democratic foreign policy expert Karl Lamers, brought exactly that message to Paris this month after an unusually cool Franco-German summit in Poitiers on June 13, just after Jospin took office, exposed the depth of mutual suspicion.

The failure to agree on anything in Poitiers was followed by a difficult Amsterdam EU summit in which France and Germany were on opposite sides both on a resolution on promoting growth and jobs, and on some aspects of reforming European institutions.
Bonn's conservative rulers saw Jospin's red-pink-and-green coalition, complete with Communist ministers, as a throwback to the bad old days of "tax and spend" socialism.

In Paris, ministers grumbled at the perceived arrogance of German leaders and Budesbank officials lecturing other Europeans on budget deficits. National Assembly speaker Laurent Fabius chose a conference on Franco-German relations to reject what he called such "decimal fetishism".
Yet Lamers said he was convinced Jospin would come round to making a further effort to cut his deficit because a failure to launch EMU would have terrible consequences for France.

"I never said it was important to reach exactly 3.0 percent. There can be unforseen factors that get in the way. But governments must display clear determination to achieve this goal," Lamers told Reuters in a July 1 interview.
"There is an urgent need for a fundamental discussion to get to the bottom of the issues on which we have differed and in some cases still differ," he said.
French Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine began the repair work in talks with his German counterpart, Klaus Kinkel, capped by a much photographed bike ride along the Rhine river two weeks ago.

European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici, a close Jospin associate keen to ensure French voters get the left-wing policies they voted for, made the pilgrimage to Cologne on Wednesday to meet his German opposite number, Werner Hoyer.
And Strauss-Kahn, a rare German-speaker in France's ruling elite, is expected to attend the Bayreuth Wagner festival later this month with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to strengthen ties.
But the vital relationship on which the sensitive EMU project may hinge will be the rapport between Kohl and Jospin, who are as different as chalk and cheese.

The expansive, Catholic Rhinelander who feels an emotional bond with France and the austere, Protestant intellectual who speaks English and Italian but has no special warmth for Germany have little in common.
Kohl made a friendly gesture on Saturday by sending Jospin personal 60th birthday greetings, saying he was sure of the French leader's determination to build a united Europe.
"It isn't a love match, but there's no reason why it shouldn't be a marriage of reason," the diplomat said.
